=== Voltus Comments on 58000.docx ===
PROJECT NO. 58000


Voltus appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposal for publication of amendments to §25.192 and §25.193 and new §25.252. Commission Staff have accurately identified the core weaknesses of the 4CP methodology: it incorrectly allocates the charges among stakeholders and creates a mismatch between the timing of its cost-recovery signal and the actual timing of system stress. Any successor methodology must both fairly allocate costs on a sound cost-causation basis and induce curtailment when it is genuinely grid-relieving rather than merely bill-reducing. Voltus agrees with this framing, but does not believe a 12CP structure achieves it. Spreading peaks evenly across all twelve months reintroduces the same disconnect in a different form: it rewards curtailment in months of little or no system stress, which neither reflects cost causation nor delivers grid relief, while diluting the signal in the months that matter most. 

Alberta offers a live example of this. AESO operates an energy-only market structurally similar to ERCOT's and has run a 12 Coincident Peak (12CP)  transmission cost recovery framework for many years; it is now actively reforming that framework after finding it drives exactly the outcome described above. A more targeted 8 Coincident Peak (8CP) approach, concentrating measured monthly peaks in the months when system stress is actually highest, avoids this failure while still meeting cost-causation and efficient-use-signal objectives.

12CP in Other Jurisdictions
Much like the ERCOT region, the AESO is an energy-only market structure and currently utilizes a 12CP framework for transmission cost recovery. There is an effort to reform this 12CP approach, as evidence suggests that a single monthly interval - particularly during shoulder months - fails to accurately capture periods of maximum peak demand. During the “shoulder seasons” of fall and spring, the peak is more difficult to capture because milder weather means that load is close to the same nearly every day. During these periods, monthly peaks are frequently established within a narrow 50-100 MW margin, even as total system demand remains at a variance of over 15% from the annual maximum. As such, incentives are completely misaligned: commercial and industrial sites must curtail for more hours during the shoulder seasons than they do during summer and winter. This misalignment results in excessive uneconomic curtailments for end-use customers during the shoulder season, and lower curtailment during the summer and winter seasons when it is actually needed. Furthermore, persistent year-round curtailment signals artificially depress energy prices, diminishing the economic incentive for essential new generation investment. Under the 12CP approach, ERCOT would have called peaks when load was <80% from maximum annual peak during 4 months in 2025 and 5 months in 2024. During these months, commercial and industrial customers would have significantly increased the number of curtailments to capture the peaks because system load was nearly the same every day. 

Recommendation
Based on Voltus's operational experience with 12CP frameworks, Voltus recommends replacing the 4 Coincident Peak (4CP) methodology with a 8CP methodology with 6 monthly peaks from May to October and 2 floating peaks from November to April. Over the last five years, the highest-demand interval of the winter season has achieved less than 10% variance from the summer peak demand, particularly during severe winter weather events in Texas which occur once or twice per year (See Figure 1). 

Figure 1 - This figure illustrates the percentage of variance relative to each annual maximum peak. The data underscores the potential for winter demand - during extreme weather events - and loads in May to approach summer peak levels. 

While system load typically remains significantly lower throughout the remainder of the season, the inclusion of two floating peaks provides a robust mechanism to target the specific winter days that approach maximum system demand. Imposing monthly peaks during periods where demand variance remains under 15% would diminish customer participation in the program and would induce curtailment that is not genuinely grid-relieving undermining the Commission’s objective of fair cost allocation. Additionally, this framework would trigger excessive curtailment events, leading to inefficient utilization of flexible demand and the artificial suppression of energy price signals. Additionally, system demand data from the preceding five-year period demonstrates that demand during May and October has surged, with variance narrowing to under 10% variance (See Figure 1). Given the shifting climatic landscape that has extended summer temperatures and load conditions into May and October, Voltus proposes the formal adoption of monthly coincident peaks for May and October, in addition to the existing June-September peaks. Such a framework ensures meaningful contributions to grid reliability precisely when the system is most vulnerable to winter storm conditions and maximum summer demand hours while ensuring balanced and purposeful demand response from end-use customers. 

Bulleted list covering each substantive recommendation:
Transition from the existing monthly 4CP framework to include up to 2 additional monthly peaks in May and October.
Add up to 2 floating peaks during the winter months (November - April).
